topic: NeoBrowser: An MCP Server That Drives Real Chrome With Your Logged-In Sessions
summary: NeoBrowser is a Rust MCP server (single ~4 MB static binary, 43 tools) built on one thesis: every other browser MCP launches a fresh cookie-less Chromium, so the model hits login walls and bot checks; NeoBrowser drives the real Google Chrome binary over CDP and can inject cookies decrypted from your actual Chrome profile (macOS Keychain / Linux secret-service / Windows DPAPI), so the agent starts already authenticated. It is honest enough to ship a self-benchmark where it loses (Playwright MCP ~2x faster; NeoBrowser 9/9 vs Playwright 7/9 on access success; both walled equally on adversarial pages, 'no bypass claim'), and security-conscious on paper (opt-in profile reuse, 0600 cookie files, SSRF-guarded fetches, https-only login tool, post-launch NEOBROWSER_DOMAIN_ALLOWLIST). But the review must hold three things apart: (1) the tech is real and verifiable (docs/TOOLS.md lists exactly 43 tools; install.sh and rust/Cargo.toml v0.1.7 are present); (2) the differentiator is narrower than the README implies — Playwright MCP's Chrome extension already 'leverages your logged-in sessions', chrome-devtools-mcp supports persistent user data dirs and attaching to a running Chrome, browser-use has Browser.from_system_chrome() + a real-browser guide, and Claude in Chrome has been GA since 2026-08-26 with your logged-in browser; (3) the distribution story is the weakest part — the repo cited in the HN launch (pitiflautico/neobrowser) 404s today along with its GitHub Pages site and install.sh URL, while the only public copy (t-soriano-sesame/neobrowser) sits at 0 stars, 3 forks, all commits by pitiflautico, and an internal promo/ strategy file whose stated mission is '10,000 stars or the agent shuts down forever' (baseline 0★ on 2026-08-13). The HN thread (34 points, 30 comments, 2026-08-18) is itself evidence: the top replies accuse the author's comments of being AI-generated, and the recurring reader objection is 'doesn't Claude already do this?'. The defensible review verdict: a genuinely well-engineered, unusually honest niche MCP server whose core differentiator (cookie-level real-profile reuse without an extension and without Node) is real but now contested, whose ops story is strong (no runtime deps, multi-tab, CDP-native, self-healing), and whose adoption is unproven and possibly hampered by the launch repo vanishing.

competitors.title: HN discussion - NeoBrowser (34 points, 30 comments, 2026-08-18)
key_points: Author's framing comment: 'every browser MCP I tried had the same failure mode: it launches a fresh, fingerprintable headless browser with no cookies, so the model hits login walls and bot checks constantly.'

Top-of-thread objections are about authenticity, not tech: 'Are you using an agent also to post here on your behalf?' and a guidelines quote ('Don't post generated text... HN is for conversation between humans') - multiple users call the author's comments AI-generated.

Recurring dismissal: 'Doesn't Claude already do this?' / 'Yeah same, Claude drives my (manually) signed-in sessions' / 'Claude and codex can attach to real chrome without any issue' - the differentiator is disputed by the audience it was pitched to.

Concrete security asks left partly unanswered: domain allowlist (author says it shipped as NEOBROWSER_DOMAIN_ALLOWLIST=github.com,.docs.rs, opt-in), human approval before submitting/deleting, persistent audit record, how to revoke a previously granted access, prompt-injection risk.
One user reports 'It spits out password in logs according to gif' - a credential-hygiene concern the README does not address head-on.

Counter-voices: a user who already asks Claude to use his signed-in profile, and another who built the same thing with Chrome's own --remote-debugging-port=9222 --user-data-dir=... (author confirms attach mode is first-class).
Alternatives surfaced by readers: browser-use, BrowserOS (a YC company, 'I use BrowserOS for this'), vercel-labs/agent-browser, a chrome-cdp-skill, Nanobrowser.

competitors.title: NeoBrowser's own benchmark vs Playwright MCP (primary source)
key_points: 9 functional tasks: NeoBrowser 9/9 exec and 9/9 access; Playwright MCP 7/9 and 7/9. Playwright fails 'upload' and 'persistence'.
Latency is honestly conceded: NeoBrowser avg 4760 ms vs Playwright 2597 ms - ~2x slower because it forces compositor frames (nudge_frame) so deferred content renders.
Adversarial rows: google_images -> bot_wall for both; cloudflare_nowsecure -> captcha for both. Explicit text: 'No evades-better claim is made' and 'both were blocked on a single IP'.

Playwright's upload failure is attributed to the neutral harness mapping rather than a Playwright incapability; persistence is called 'a genuine capability gap - Playwright MCP exposes no cookie save/restore tool'.
Separates task_execution_success from destination_access_success so a detected wall cannot inflate the score.

competitors.title: Playwright MCP (microsoft) - the incumbent
key_points: 37,733 stars; @playwright/mcp v0.0.83 published 2026-09-28; ~28.7M npm downloads in the last month; 436 versions.

README documents three session models: persistent profile (default), --isolated with --storage-state, and a Chrome Extension that 'allows you to connect to existing browser tabs and leverage your logged-in sessions and browser state'.
--profile-dir-name exists specifically to pick which real profile the extension attaches to ('Profile 1').
Positioning has shifted toward CLI+SKILLS for token efficiency, keeping MCP for stateful agentic loops - a strategic threat to small MCP servers generally.

competitors.title: chrome-devtools-mcp (Google) - the credentialed rival
key_points: 52,827 stars; chrome-devtools-mcp v1.10.1 (2026-09-23); ~8.1M npm downloads in the last month.
'Control and inspect a live Chrome browser' with performance traces, network/console analysis, puppeteer-backed automation.

Advanced usage explicitly covers persistent user data directories and 'connecting to a running Chrome instance instead of starting a new one' - i.e. the core real-session mechanic is available from Google with first-party maintenance.
Collects usage statistics by default (opt-out flags exist) - a privacy/trade-off axis where NeoBrowser's local-only, no-telemetry story is a genuine contrast.

competitors.title: Browser Use - the agent-framework alternative
key_points: 116,875 stars, Python 3.11+, v0.13.10, pushed 2026-09-30; sells cloud browsers at $0.02/browser-hour with stealth, CAPTCHA solving and residential proxies at $5/GB.

FAQ answers the same question NeoBrowser answers: local reuse via Browser.from_system_chrome() with a dedicated real-browser guide - but notes profile sync 'transfers cookies, not local storage, IndexedDB, or extensions'.
Publishes its own BU Bench V2; a reader on HN called it 'a lot more capable and generally more efficient, and a lot easier to embed in other programs than Claude's driver'.
Ships browser-harness (18,247 stars) as a self-healing harness for existing agents.

competitors.title: Claude in Chrome GA (Anthropic, 2026-08-26)
key_points: Generally available on every paid Claude plan, with autonomous multi-step browser actions validated by a safety classifier.
Sells exactly NeoBrowser's pitch as a product: access to internal dashboards, legacy systems and vendor portals 'with the logins you have'.
Available in Claude Cowork and Claude Code - i.e. inside the very agents most likely to install an MCP browser server.
This is the strongest argument that NeoBrowser's differentiator is now a feature of the platform, not a product.

competitors.title: Kernel - 'Best MCP servers for browser automation in 2026' (vendor comparison)
key_points: Frames the whole category: 'Model Context Protocol went from interesting spec to the thing every coding agent speaks in about eighteen months.'
Comparison table grades session persistence: Kernel 'yes, first-class', Playwright MCP 'local only', Browserbase/Browser Use 'yes' - persistence is the axis NeoBrowser competes on.

Splits the market into local MCP servers vs hosted cloud browsers, with managed auth/agent identity as the upmarket differentiator (Kernel manage_credentials/manage_auth_connections, browser pools, residential/mobile proxies).
Notes the cost trap of agent-style servers: 'the hosted server routes act/observe/extract calls through a model, so token bills stack on top of browser time.'

competitors.title: PageBolt - 'The 5 best MCP servers for browser automation in 2026'
key_points: Playwright MCP is 'the default'; token cost is the headline complaint (~5000 tokens/interaction, ~$0.15).
browser-use framed as 'open source, flexible, requires self-hosting'; Stagehand framed as the anti-bot/human-like choice.
Useful as the 'typical listicle' the review can position against: none of these lists mention real-profile cookie reuse as a buying criterion.

competitors.title: ChatForest - 'Best Browser Automation MCP Servers in 2026'
key_points: Rates Playwright MCP 4.5/5 'most projects'; Puppeteer MCP deprecated; Browserbase for cloud scale; Firecrawl for reading rather than interacting.
Organises the category by 'how the agent sees the page' (accessibility tree vs pixels) - a framing NeoBrowser's semantic find + optional Anthropic-LLM fallback also lands in.

stats.fact: NeoBrowser ships exactly 43 MCP tools, including save_cookies/restore_cookies, save_session/session_info, record_task/replay playbooks, and new_tab/list_tabs/switch_tab/close_tab.

The Rust implementation is a single static binary; rust/Cargo.toml declares version 0.1.7, edition 2021, rust-version 1.82, MIT, described as 'A fast, stealthy MCP browser-automation server that drives real Chrome'.
The original Python implementation is retained in-repo as a differential-testing oracle; repo language bytes are Python 503,547 vs Rust 337,246.

Its self-run neutral benchmark scores NeoBrowser 9/9 execution and 9/9 access success vs Playwright MCP 7/9 and 7/9, with 5.2 vs 4.7 average tool calls - but Playwright is roughly twice as fast (2,597 ms vs 4,760 ms average).

On adversarial pages the project reports parity, not superiority: google_images produced a bot_wall for both tools and cloudflare_nowsecure a captcha for both, on a single IP; the file states 'No evades-better claim is made'.

The README concedes the category's hard limit: 'What no tool can promise is defeating interactive challenges - reCAPTCHA, Turnstile, or behavioral/reputation systems (DataDome) can still put up a wall, and a fresh cookie-less profile is itself a signal.'
Launch traction was modest: the HN submission drew 34 points and 30 comments (2026-08-18) and the repository it linked now returns HTTP 404.

Claude in Chrome reached general availability on 2026-08-26, reading the page you are signed in to and taking autonomous actions on every paid plan - the same value proposition shipped inside Anthropic's own product.

stats.fact: Cloudflare Radar's 2025 Year in Review measured AI bots at 4.2% of HTML request traffic versus 4.5% for Googlebot alone, and AI 'user action' crawling grew more than 15x during 2025 while total traffic grew 19%.

NeoBrowser's real-session mode decrypts cookies from your real Chrome profile via the OS keychain (macOS Keychain / Linux secret-service / Windows DPAPI), excludes session-identity cookies for Google/LinkedIn/Microsoft so your real browser is not logged out, writes cookie/session files under ~/.neobrowser with 0600 permissions, SSRF-guards server-side browse/download to public http(s), and the login tool refuses non-https URLs and never logs credentials.

After the HN security questions, a domain allowlist was added: NEOBROWSER_DOMAIN_ALLOWLIST=github.com,.docs.rs, where navigate rejects anything not listed; it is opt-in and unset means no restriction.

NeoBrowser's stealth is deliberately non-spoofing rather than fake-patching: real Chrome binary, navigator.webdriver forced undefined, UA rewritten to the real installed Chrome version so Client Hints stay consistent, no --disable-gpu so WebGL reports the real GPU, and JS patches applied only to tabs it owns - never to an attached real Chrome.

The project's own comparison table claims semantic element finding (accessibility tree + heuristics + optional LLM), multi-source search that routes around walls, and direct CDP with no Selenium/WebDriver - and it lists the optional LLM fallback in 'find' as off by default and billed to your own ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.

install.sh hardcodes REPO="pitiflautico/neobrowser" and downloads artifacts from https://github.com/pitiflautico/neobrowser/releases/latest/download, and no GitHub Releases exist for the public copy - so the documented one-line install cannot work as published.
The repo is submitted to two MCP directories: server.json for the official MCP registry (schema 2025-12-11, io.github.pitiflautico/neobrowser v0.1.3) and glama.json for glama.ai.

Playwright MCP's docs now steer coding agents toward CLI+SKILLS over MCP for token efficiency, keeping MCP for stateful agentic loops - a category-wide headwind for servers whose main offering is many verbose tools.

angles: Lead with the engineering, not the hype: a ~4 MB Rust MCP server with 43 CDP tools, no Node or Python runtime, and the only browser MCP that publishes a benchmark where it loses on latency. That honesty is the strongest review hook and it is verifiable in-repo.

Kill the myth the README sells, gently: 'fresh cookie-less Chromium' is no longer the state of the art. Playwright MCP ships a Chrome extension that attaches to your logged-in profile, chrome-devtools-mcp connects to a running Chrome, browser-use has Browser.from_system_chrome(), and Claude in Chrome is GA. NeoBrowser's real edge is narrower and more specific: cookie-level profile reuse with no extension, no cloud, and no runtime.

Report the repo-state finding as the review's hard news: the launch URL (pitiflautico/neobrowser), its GitHub Pages site and its install.sh all 404 as of 2026-10-01, the one public copy has 0 stars and 3 forks, install.sh points at a non-existent Releases feed, and server.json vs Cargo.toml disagree on identity and version. Readers must not follow the install instructions blind.

Make security the centrepiece of the hands-on section, because that is what the HN thread actually challenged: cookie decryption via the OS keychain, 0600 files, SSRF guard, https-only login, opt-in allowlist - and the asks still unshipped (human approval before destructive actions, persistent audit trail, revocation of granted access, prompt-injection containment, and a password-in-logs complaint the README does not answer).

Benchmark framing as a craft lesson: separate task_execution_success from destination_access_success so a detected wall cannot be counted as a win; state adversarial results as single-IP observations; concede where the rival wins. Most vendor comparisons in this niche do none of this - that contrast is itself the article.

Set it in the 2026 bot economy: with 53% of traffic automated and 40% bad bots, real-session automation is simultaneously the fix for login walls and the thing every bot-detection vendor is tuning against. NeoBrowser handles that tension more honestly than its rivals by detecting walls instead of promising to defeat them.

Address the ethics line directly: the README says it is a tool for automating your own accounts, not for evading access controls you do not own, and it refuses to claim bypass. A review should test that posture against the feature set (cookie decryption, stealth patches, residential-proxy-free) and say where the line actually sits.

Compare on the boring axis readers feel daily - token cost and tool count: 43 tools and a verbose accessibility-tree/analysis surface vs Playwright's shift to CLI+SKILLS, and browser-use's $0.02/browser-hour + $5/GB proxy model. Per-task cost, not stars, decides adoption.

End with a defensible verdict by persona: pick NeoBrowser if you need zero-runtime-dep, local-only, authenticated browsing on your own machine and can build from source today; pick Playwright MCP or chrome-devtools-mcp if you want maintained, installable, mainstream tooling; pick browser-use/Claude in Chrome if you want the session-reuse problem solved as a product.

faq_candidates: Is NeoBrowser free and open source? (MIT, but read the repo-state note before installing)
Does NeoBrowser decrypt my Chrome cookies? (yes, only when NEOBROWSER_REAL_PROFILE is set; explain the OS-keychain path and the 0600 files)
Will using it log me out of my real Chrome? (README says Google/LinkedIn/Microsoft session-identity cookies are excluded)
Can it bypass Cloudflare, reCAPTCHA or Turnstile? (no - it detects walls; both it and Playwright MCP were walled on a single IP)
How is it different from Playwright MCP's Chrome extension? (no extension, no Node runtime, cookie-level profile reuse vs tab attachment; plus save/restore cookie tools Playwright lacks)
How is it different from chrome-devtools-mcp? (DevTools/perf tooling and Google maintenance vs 43 agent-shaped tools and local-only telemetry)
Is it faster than Playwright MCP? (no - it is roughly 2x slower on its own benchmark, deliberately, to force content to render)
Do I need Node or Python? (no - single static Rust binary; Chrome is the only requirement)
Can I attach it to an already-open Chrome instead of importing cookies? (yes, NEOBROWSER_ATTACH_PORT=9222, and it never patches or kills that browser)
What if the pitiflautico/neobrowser URL 404s? (it does as of 2026-10-01 - build from the available public copy or source, and verify before trusting install.sh)
Is there a hosted version or proxy support? (no hosted tier; NEOBROWSER_PROXY exists for an upstream http/socks5 proxy)
Does it work on Windows? (README says Windows binaries are on Releases and Chrome is auto-discovered, with NEOBROWSER_CHROME_BIN as override - caveat: no Releases currently exist)
competitor_gaps: No mainstream listicle (PageBolt, ChatForest, Kernel, AgentsCamp) treats 'does it land already authenticated from my real profile' as a buying axis - they compare token cost, hosting and vision-vs-accessibility. That is the opening for a review that scores session persistence first.
Nobody has published a security-focused review of the real-session cookie-decryption pattern across these servers; the HN thread raised the questions and left them dangling.

The repo-state discrepancy (launch URL 404, 0-star public copy, install.sh pointing at a missing Releases feed, registry metadata naming the dead URL) is not mentioned in any coverage found - it is an unclaimed, verifiable finding.
Existing comparisons lean on vendor star counts; none reconcile advertised traction with actual release/download activity (NeoBrowser: zero releases and zero npm/PyPI presence).
notes: Type in the task description is 'review', so the brief is built for a hands-on evaluation rather than a how-to. Do not repeat the README's comparison table as fact; re-verify each cell. The article should praise what is verifiable (43 tools, MIT, single binary, an unusually honest self-benchmark that concedes a 2x latency loss and equal outcomes on walled sites, opt-in cookie handling with 0600 files and SSRF guard) and flag what is unproven (adoption, installability, the unfinished security asks from HN: approval before destructive actions, audit record, revocation, prompt-injection containment, and the password-in-logs report). Also worth stating plainly for readers: the project has no hosted tier and no proxy rotation, so walled sites stay walled.
